children.text: arkiv is a shared photo archive pinned to a 3D globe. People add a photo with a title, a caption, the date it was taken and a pin where it happened. Everyone else browses the globe and moves from one photo to the next through what they have in common.

alt: arkiv's explore view: a lime globe on a white page, covered in peach photo dots joined by thin periwinkle lines

children.text: Solo: research, UX and UI design, brand, front end, back end and deployment.
v1: December 2024, final project for Networks and Navigation (CART 351) at Concordia. v2: redesign, November 2026.
Figma, React, Mapbox GL JS, Cloudinary, MongoDB Atlas, Vercel
the brief

Networks and Navigation looks at how people move through connected information: links, maps, paths and the structures behind them. For the final project I wanted a dataset where the network was made of something personal, so I chose photos of places and the days they were taken.
arkiv treats every photo as a node with three properties: who took it, where, and when. Two photos are connected when they share a day or an author. The globe handles
where
, and the connections handle
who
and
when
. Navigating arkiv means moving through that network rather than scrolling a feed.
Photos, each with an author, a date and a location.
Same day: every photo taken on that date. Same author: one person's photos in date order.
Rotate and zoom the globe to find a place, then follow edges from photo to photo.
the problem with v1
v1 proved the idea and met the brief, but it was hard to use on both sides: adding a photo and looking through them.

images.alt: arkiv v1: a gray globe with yellow dots and dark connection lines
arkiv v1 landing page with the words click a dot repeated in blue
arkiv v1 photo details listing date, country, photographer and equipment above the photo

children.text: browsing dead-ended.
Opening a photo showed its details and nothing else. The network existed only as lines drawn on the map.
the lines carried no information.
Every photo from the same day was joined to every other one, so a busy date became a mesh of crossing lines you couldn't act on.
uploading asked for too much.

Eight fields: title, photographer, story, date, country, email, equipment and the image. Country was typed by hand even though the pin already set the location, and email and equipment were never shown.
it wasn't built for phones.
Only the form and header had small-screen adjustments. The map and the photo popup had none.
private data was exposed.
The API sent every entry's email address to every visitor, and nothing told contributors their submission would be public.
users and goals
arkiv has two kinds of use, and most people do both.
Wants to add a photo of a place and a day quickly, often from a phone.
Needs few fields, an easy way to set the location and clear feedback.
v1 failed them with eight fields, a typed country and no phone layout.
Wants to find something interesting and keep going.
Needs a reason to open the next photo after this one.
v1 failed them with dead-ended photo details and unreadable lines.

User testing during the redesign shaped two of the biggest changes: phone sizes and layouts were the main problem people ran into, and sorting by recent came out of testing too. The visual identity was a separate, solo rebrand.
goals
Every photo leads to at least one other photo.
An upload fits on one screen, on desktop and on phone.
No view needs scrolling, apart from very long captions.
Collect only what the site shows, and say clearly that it is public.
constraints
Solo project: every feature had to be something one person could design, build and maintain.
Existing v1 entries had to keep working without a data migration.
The globe is a Mapbox map, so its look, gestures and performance set limits on the explore view.
structure and flows
v1 opened straight onto the map, with upload as a separate page. v2 keeps the same two jobs and makes them the first choice: the landing page is split into upload and explore.

alt: arkiv's landing page split into a gray upload half and a peach explore half, with the arkiv wordmark on the seam

children.text: 1. Explore opens on the slowly turning globe.
2. Hover a dot to see its title; click it to open its card.
3. The card shows the photo, title, author, date, place and a short caption.
4. Arrows step to the next linked photo, by date, author or most recent.
5. Expand to see the full photo and caption.
1. Add a photo: drag, browse or take one with the camera.
2. Fill in title, caption, author and date.
3. Drop a pin on the globe, or use your current location.
4. Upload, then see it on the globe or upload another.
On phones, steps 1–2 and step 3 are two separate screens.
key decisions
1. browse through connections, not a list
problem.
in v1, opening a photo was a dead end.
options.
a grid or feed of recent photos; search and filters; or keep the globe and make the links between photos navigable.
decision.
keep the globe as the only view and let people move along the edges. A switch sets what "related" means: same day (
date
) or same person (
author
recent
toggle, added after user testing, orders every photo newest first. Arrows on the card step through the set, with a count like "3 of 5 · same author".
trade-off.
there is no way to search for a specific photo, person or place. With a small archive that's acceptable; it won't be as the archive grows.

alt: a photo card open in author mode, with periwinkle lines tracing the same author's photos across the map
caption: connect by author: one person's photos form a trail in date order

children.text: 2. make the lines readable
problem.
v1 drew every relationship at once, so the lines carried no usable information.
options.
remove the lines; show them only for the open photo; show one kind of relationship at a time.
decision.

one kind at a time, chosen by the date / author switch. Author links are drawn as a single chain in date order, so one person's photos read as a route. Lines are thin and light so the dots stay the main target.
trade-off.
date mode still links every pair of photos from that day, so a very busy day can still get dense.
3. show the photo next to where it is
problem.
details need space, but covering the globe hides where the photo was taken.
options.
a modal over the globe; a fixed side panel; a card beside the dot.
decision.

a card on the right of the screen, with the globe moving so the dot sits to its left and a thin line joining them. On phones the card becomes a sheet along the bottom and the dot moves to the top of the screen.
trade-off.
the globe has to move every time a photo opens, which can be disorienting when stepping quickly between distant photos.

alt: a photo of a street in Havana open in its card, joined by a thin line to its dot on the globe
caption: a photo opened from its dot

children.text: 4. ask for five fields and a pin
problem.
the v1 form had eight fields, and three of them added work without adding anything visible.
options.
keep the fields but make some optional; or remove everything the site doesn't display.
decision.
photo, title, caption, author and date, plus a pin. Country is looked up from the pin. Email and equipment are removed.
trade-off.
less metadata per photo, and the country depends on a reverse-geocoding lookup.

alt: the upload page: a drop zone and four fields on the left, a small globe for dropping a pin on the right

children.text: 5. set location with a pin
problem.
typing a country or address is slow and error-prone, especially on a phone.
options.
an address search; a pin on a map; the device's location.
decision.
click a small globe to drop or move the pin, or use the device's location in one tap.
trade-off.
no place search yet, so finding a small town on a small globe takes some zooming.
6. split upload into two steps on phones
problem.
in testing, phone sizes and layouts were the biggest problem. The photo box, four fields and a globe don't fit on a phone screen together.
options.
one scrolling form; or two steps.
decision.
two steps, "photo & details" then "location". Step one is checked before moving on, and if anything is missing at submit, the form returns to that step.
trade-off.
one extra tap, in exchange for each step fitting without scrolling.

images.alt: arkiv on a phone: a photo card as a sheet along the bottom of the screen
arkiv on a phone: step one of the upload form

caption: explore and upload on a phone

children.text: 7. fit the card without scrolling
problem.
photos come in any shape and captions in any length, but a card that scrolls is hard to step through quickly.
decision.
the photo keeps its own aspect ratio and gives up height when the text needs room. Captions are cut to three lines, with the full caption one tap away.
trade-off.
most captions are truncated in the card.
8. use colour for meaning, not decoration
problem.
v1's bright colours competed with the photos. This was part of the solo rebrand, not a testing finding.
decision.

a soft three-colour palette where each colour has one meaning: lime for land, peach for photos (the dots), periwinkle for connections and links. Early v2 versions with gradients and glows were flattened to solid colour.
trade-off.

lime can't be used for text (about 1.1:1 on white), so periwinkle carries text accents. Card text is set in a soft gray (#AEAEAE) on purpose so it sits behind the photo, at the cost of lower contrast than body text.
9. let the globe move, but not while you're using it
problem.
a slowly spinning globe signals that it's interactive, but it also moves things out from under the pointer.
decision.
the spin stops on press, waits 1.2 seconds after a zoom before resuming, and pauses while hovering a dot, while a card is open and when zoomed in. It's off with reduced motion.
10. be clear about what's public
problem.
v1 sent contributors' email addresses to every visitor and never said submissions were public.
decision.
the API now returns only the fields the site shows, email is no longer collected, and the information panel states that everything added is public.
trade-off.
v1 entries may still hold emails in the database, and those should be deleted.
design system

The rebrand is documented as a design system: three brand colours with fixed roles, ABC Areal in lowercase throughout, square corners and ten components. It's written up in the brand book in the repository.
Land on the globe and accents. Never text.
Photo dots, button hover tint and invalid fields.
Connections, links, active controls and button borders.
outcome and next steps
v2 is live. Against the goals:
every photo leads to another:
met when a photo shares a day or an author; a photo with neither only leads on through
recent
upload fits one screen:
met on desktop, and on phones in two steps.
no scrolling:
met, except long captions in the full view.
collect only what's shown and say it's public:
met for new uploads; old v1 data still to clean up.
next
Add place search to the pin picker.
Add a way to find a specific photo or person as the archive grows.
Moderation: anyone can upload, and there's currently no way to report or remove a photo.
